#5109. One Bitcoin miner paid an $11.9M tariff bill four years after delivery

Bitcoin mining companies are still resolving customs disputes over machines that entered the US years ago.

Bitcoin miner Bitfarms thought the machines it brought into Washington state in 2021 had been made in Malaysia. Its supplier said so, and the company provided US Customs officials with documents supporting that claim.

Four years later, the company paid the government $11.9 million. US Customs and Border Protection had challenged the machines' declared origin, arguing that they were made in China and subject to a 25% import duty.

Bitfarms disputed the assessment, but its financial statements show it paid in October 2025, after Customs told it the duties were required.

The payment shows a cost that can follow a mining company long after its equipment was delivered and started working. Other miners have faced similar disputes over where their machines were made, with one company recently avoiding a potential $100 million assessment and another still contesting an estimate that reached $130 million.

Those numbers don't add up to a single bill for the industry. Each dispute involves different shipments, documents, and decisions, and the outcomes can look very different even when the companies believe they have evidence supporting their declared origins.

Bitfarms' dispute began in early 2022, when Customs challenged the origin of the machines imported the previous year. The company said its Chinese vendor had represented that the equipment came from Malaysia, while Customs asserted that it was manufactured in China.

The miner submitted supporting documents in the third quarter of 2023 and again in the first quarter of 2025. It also paid $180,000 of the duties in 2024, according to its later filing. As of June 2025, management said it didn't consider a future cash outflow probable and hadn't recorded a provision for the dispute.

That was an accounting assessment based on what the company knew at the time. In August 2025, Customs responded that duties were required, and Bitfarms reported the payment two months later.

Bitfarms disclosed $180,000 of customs duties paid in 2024 and a separate $11.9 million payment to Customs in October 2025, including interest. The filing’s stated duties and interest components do not reconcile to its reported October payment.

Source: Bitfarms September 2025 financial statements, customs duties note

The company hasn't disclosed enough to reconstruct every step of the customs process or establish whether it paid under protest. Nonetheless, its filings do show how a dispute over a shipment can remain relevant to a company's finances long after the initial purchase.

Company disclosures trace the disputed origin of mining equipment from its arrival in 2021 to a payment in October 2025.

The purchase year did not determine when Bitfarms would pay the customs assessment.

Based on company disclosures, not the underlying Customs correspondence. The October payment included interest. The filing does not establish every procedural step or whether payment was under protest.

Timeline transcribed from Note 16 of Bitfarms September 2025 financial statements. Dollar figures converted from the stated thousands of US dollars. Milestones are equally spaced for readability, not elapsed time.

Based on company disclosures, not the underlying Customs correspondence. The October payment included interest. The filing does not establish every procedural step or whether payment was under protest.

Bitfarms has since reorganized under Keel Infrastructure and shifted toward AI and high-performance computing. It paid the customs bill before that transition reached a major milestone: Keel stopped its US Bitcoin mining operations in June 2026 as it prepared sites for other uses.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

Other miners have also been shifting power access and data-center sites toward AI, while older import disputes still appear in their financial disclosures.

The money involved can affect how much they have available for equipment and projects, although a disclosed potential charge isn't necessarily money they will have to pay.

Import duties can depend on where a product was made, which sounds simple until a machine contains components from several countries and is assembled elsewhere.

US customs forms ask importers to identify the product's country of origin. When production takes place in more than one country, the answer can depend on where the product underwent its last substantial transformation, according to Customs' entry instructions.

The manufacturing process and supporting records can affect the duty owed. The supplier's certificate can support the declared origin, but Customs can still challenge it.

Equipment can also be released and put to work before Customs resolves every issue. Customs uses a process called liquidation to make its final duty calculation for an entry.

Importers can challenge certain decisions through an administrative protest, but deadlines and exceptions depend on the decision being challenged. The public filings don't establish which procedural rules explain every stage of the miners' disputes.

Selling the equipment doesn't automatically settle an importer's customs obligations either. Federal regulations describe duties as a debt owed by the importer, which can be discharged through payment or applicable legal relief.

That doesn't mean the buyer of a secondhand machine automatically inherits the seller's customs bill, since the importer and the terms of any transaction need to be identified separately.

IREN received a notice in April 2025 concerning hardware it imported between April 2024 and February 2025. Customs asserted that the equipment was of Chinese origin and assessed a 25% tariff, while IREN said the seller and shipping documents supported a different origin.

The company contested an exposure of approximately $100 million. In October 2026, Customs approved its protests and accepted the declared origin of the covered hardware, IREN reported in its September-quarter filing. No additional tariff, administrative fee, or interest is payable for that matter.

The $100 million was an amount IREN had disputed and no longer has to pay for the covered imports. The company hasn't disclosed enough about the decision to establish whether the same reasoning applies to other shipments or other miners.

CleanSpark has had a mixed outcome so far. In its June-quarter filing, submitted in August, the miner said Customs had approved some of its protests over machines imported in 2024, while other entries remained contested.

If Customs prevailed on the remaining entries, CleanSpark estimated that its total tariff liability for the previously purchased machines could reach approximately $130 million, excluding interest. Management considered a loss improbable and recorded no provision as of June 30.

DarkHorse Technologies, previously known as Sphere 3D, faces a smaller claim that shows how an older equipment purchase can appear in the accounts of a miner with a different name and business plan.

In August, Customs notified DarkHorse that it was asserting Chinese-origin duties on machines purchased in 2022 by a subsidiary acquired in the Cathedra Bitcoin combination.

The company says its subsidiary received certificates from the seller supporting a non-Chinese origin, and it filed a protest in September. Its latest quarterly report puts potential liability at up to $2.3 million, including interest, if Customs prevails. DarkHorse has not recorded a liability.

Company estimates if Customs prevails. CleanSpark's was approximately $130 million excluding interest as of June 30. DarkHorse's was up to $2.3 million including interest in its Sept. 30 report. Reporting dates and interest treatment differ.

Source: CleanSpark June 2026 Form 10-Q, Note 15 · DarkHorse September 2026 Form 10-Q, customs duties contingency

DarkHorse is separately selling its legacy mining fleet as it shifts toward AI infrastructure. Its quarterly report estimated $2.9 million in proceeds, with $1.3 million from machines sold by Sept. 30.

Bitfarms reported a payment, IREN's covered assessment has been resolved, CleanSpark's estimate excludes interest, and DarkHorse's includes it. Adding them together would treat a past payment and an avoided charge as outstanding bills.

CleanSpark's remaining protests and DarkHorse's challenge will determine whether either miner faces a further payment on the disputed imports.

IREN's result shows that a challenge can succeed, while Bitfarms' earlier payment shows why investors can't assume that a company's initial accounting assessment will be the final word.

#5106. Quantum Upgrade Could Be 'Particularly Challenging' for Blockchains: IOSCO

Quantum Upgrade Could Be 'Particularly Challenging' for Blockchains: IOSCO

Financial markets, including crypto, need to start preparing now for quantum computers capable of breaking the cryptography that secures them, according to the world's main forum for securities regulators.

A "sufficiently capable" quantum computer could undermine widely used public-key cryptography that supports critical functions across financial markets, the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO) said in a report published on Thursday. The cyber readiness challenge posed by quantum computing "is immediate and requires action," it said.

"Practical quantum computers capable of compromising widely used cryptography do not yet exist, but the scale and duration of the transition mean the financial sector should start preparing today," IOSCO Board Chair Jean-Paul Servais said in a statement.

The 63-page report cited conservative estimates that such machines could emerge between 2030 and 2035. Several industry participants consulted by IOSCO went further, arguing that firms should prepare for the possibility that they arrive within five years, potentially accelerated by AI.

IOSCO said the migration may be particularly challenging for blockchains, because cryptography is embedded in their core architecture and any change requires coordinated action across decentralized networks. Public blockchains such as Ethereum, Solana and Tron rely heavily on elliptic curve cryptography to verify identities and validate transactions, and a powerful enough quantum computer could derive private keys from exposed public keys, a scenario known as "Q-Day."

Swapping in quantum-resistant signatures comes at a cost. Signatures under ML-DSA-44, a post-quantum standard from the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, are about 2,420 bytes, roughly 35 to 40 times larger than today's 64-byte elliptic curve signatures, the report said. It cited evidence from a quantum-resistant Solana testnet that saw throughput fall by about 90% when post-quantum signatures replaced existing ones.

Because the cryptography sits in transaction formats and consensus rules, replacing it requires hard forks, and decentralized networks have no way to force quick adoption, making migration "slow and fragmented," IOSCO said. Accounts and smart contracts still controlled by vulnerable keys could stay exposed after a network adds quantum-resistant options, and the path to quantum resistance for Bitcoin wallets remains uphill.

Wallet makers face their own trade-offs. SHRINCS, the leading candidate for a post-quantum Bitcoin signature scheme, offers "stateful" signatures that are about 10 times smaller but can expose funds to theft if keys are reused beyond a set signing budget, Trezor CTO Tomáš Sušánka has said. Trezor is considering making the larger, safer stateless option the default, and hardware wallets will also need post-quantum cryptography for firmware and device authentication, he added.

The report distinguished "on-spend" attacks, in which an attacker races to exploit a public key revealed by a pending transaction, from "at-rest" attacks on keys left exposed for longer. Dormant or abandoned coins pose a particular problem where their holders can't move them. Crypto firms have formed a quantum alliance as some 6 million BTC sit in exposed addresses, and Bitcoin developer Cory Fields has proposed "quantum landmines" to make attacks on such coins costly.

Layer-2 networks are not insulated either. Optimistic rollups could face forged signatures during their dispute windows, typically seven days on Ethereum, and many zero-knowledge rollups use SNARK proofs that rely on elliptic curves. Hash-based STARK proofs are more resistant, but a rollup is only as safe as the layer-1 contracts, bridges and governance keys it depends on, the report said.

Developers are already working on fixes. Researchers have proposed several ways to make Bitcoin quantum-safe, StarkWare has shown a quantum-safe Bitcoin transaction, and Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin has said the network is betting its future on quantum resistance.

IOSCO said firms should migrate to post-quantum cryptography and build "crypto-agility," the ability to update cryptographic systems without major redesign. Quantum key distribution could complement those measures on selected high-security channels, it added.

Most preparations across financial markets are still at an early stage, focused on awareness, governance, training and identifying vulnerable systems, according to the report, which drew on a March 2026 survey of members of IOSCO's Fintech Task Force and discussions with experts. Some respondents described "quantum-procrastination," in which firms put off action while waiting for clearer regulatory signals or wider adoption.

No surveyed jurisdiction reported operational deployment of quantum computing in regulated financial services. The watchdog also urged regulators to act against "quantum washing," in which firms overstate the role, maturity or performance of quantum technology. IOSCO said it will treat quantum as a priority in 2027, focusing on raising awareness across the financial ecosystem.

Quantum hardware is advancing quickly. IBM has claimed a trusted quantum advantage, and Google has said it has cracked some of the field's biggest bottlenecks.

#5101. Gen Z Embraces Crypto While Most Americans Call It a 'Side Quest'

Gen Z Embraces Crypto While Most Americans Call It a 'Side Quest'

For many young Americans, crypto is coming before the 401(k).

Some 21% of Gen Z adults own cryptocurrency, compared with 16% who hold an employer-sponsored retirement plan like a 401(k), according to a survey released Thursday by SoFi Technologies.

That’s seven times the rate of baby boomers, just 3% of whom own crypto. Crypto was Gen Z’s most widely held investment in the survey, ahead of stocks, bonds ,and real estate.

The online survey of 2,064 U.S. adults was conducted by SoFi and YouGov from Oct. 15 to 28. SoFi, a nationally chartered bank that sells crypto alongside checking and investment accounts, developed the report with Culture Co-op.

Gen Z respondents described crypto less as a gamble than a strategy. They were nearly three times as likely as the general population to call it one of the best ways to build future wealth, 21% vs. 8%, and 61% said they see it as a financial advantage unique to their generation.

Only 20% of Gen Z crypto owners said they bought in because it “sounded interesting,” compared with 34% of crypto investors overall. Diversification (32%) and easier international payments (29%) ranked higher.

Part of the gap reflects age. Many respondents in their late teens and 20s don’t yet have access to an employer retirement plan.

Across the broader population, the picture is far cooler. Only 13% of Americans own crypto, and 62% are firm skeptics. Three in four say crypto feels intimidating to get into, and 77% agreed with the statement, “Cryptocurrency feels like a financial side quest that I don’t have the time or energy for.”

Even owners feel out of their depth: 82% of current crypto investors said they should know more about it than they do, and 11% admitted knowing little to nothing.

“Nobody feels the gaps in their financial education more sharply than someone who has just bought Bitcoin,” said Natalie Brunell, host of the Coin Stories podcast and a contributor to SoFi’s crypto newsletter.

The findings echo a recent survey conducted by Ipsos for the DeFi Education Fund, which found that 22% of Americans have ever owned or used crypto but only 13% used it in the past year.

SoFi argues that putting crypto in the same app as banking is the key to wider adoption. Half of respondents open to crypto said having their primary bank offer it would be a tipping point, and 63% of current investors said they’d trade more if they could do it at their bank.

SoFi has been building out that model, launching a tokenized deposit that pays 4.4% and moves like a stablecoin, as well as a bank-issued stablecoin running on Polygon’s payments infrastructure.

The survey also challenges the crypto “tech bro” stereotype. Black and Hispanic respondents own crypto at more than twice the rate of white respondents, 22% to 9%. Miami led the 10 cities surveyed at 20% ownership, while San Francisco matched the national average at 13%.

With Thanksgiving just around the corner, I’ve already started thinking about two very important things: what’s going on the dinner table and what I’ll wear. I’m especially looking forward to my mom’s baked mashed potatoes (a family favorite) and the homemade mac and cheese I’ll be bringing along. But, especially as a style writer, half the fun of the holidays is having a good excuse to put together a good outfit.

My family’s Thanksgiving gatherings tend to be pretty casual, so I’m not one to show up in anything overly dressy or uncomfortable. I’m usually somewhere in the middle, opting for an outfit that looks like I made an effort but still lets me enjoy a second helping of stuffing without worrying about a too-tight waistband. Think a great sweater with loose-fitting jeans, a knit dress with boots, or even a smartly-styled leggings outfit. Because as much as I love dressing up for the holidays, I also want to enjoy post-dinner card games or sit comfortably on the couch afterward.

If you’re approaching Thanksgiving dressing the same way, I’ve rounded up six outfit ideas to help get you inspired. I’ve included a few options perfect for a Christmas card photoshoot, along with more laid-back looks that are just as fitting for a casual family gathering. No matter what your holiday plans look like, these outfits strike that happy medium between looking good and feeling comfortable. Now, if you’ll excuse me, I have some mac and cheese to make.

In my opinion, there’s no outfit more perfect for the holidays than a sweater dress and boots. It’s cute enough for family photos but loose and soft enough to keep you comfy all day (especially if you kick the boots off at the door). Grab a long-sleeve knit dress that hits somewhere between mid-thigh and the knee and pair it with some fleece-lined tights and your fave knee-high boot. A midi or maxi dress with an ankle bootie works too.

Start by pulling out a denim jacket and denim skirt. From there, add a plain white T-shirt. I love brown for the fall, so I wore my version of this outfit with brown boots and a matching brown belt and bag. I love this combo because it looks super stylish, but I don’t feel overdressed or uncomfortable when I wear it. Don’t have a denim skirt or jacket? No problem. You can recreate this look with a leather jacket, jeans, or any neutral mini skirt.

Start with a pair of satin or silk pants and pair them with a sweater and ballet flats in the same shade. This outfit has been one of my go-tos lately because it’s so comfortable, but the monochrome palette and shiny finish of the pants make it look like I tried way harder than I actually did. You can even make it feel a little dressier by swapping the flats for a pair of pointed-toe ankle boots.

It doesn’t get comfier than leggings and slippers. For ultra-casual gatherings when you just want to focus on family and food without looking frumpy, just style yours a little smarter. Go for a pair of leggings with minimal seaming (especially a pair without a front seam), which makes them look sleeker. Then grab a dressy-looking oversized sweater—something with a boxy cut, a turtleneck, or a nice knit. I find that my tweed stitch J. Crew Rollneck Sweater is perfect for this look. Finish it off with a neutral slipper and a pair of scrunchy socks.

Crz Yoga SculptAir No Front Seam Leggings

Opt for a pair of baggier jeans for this more casual outfit, which will be way comfier than a restrictive skinny or straight-leg jean. A looser pant also pairs better with a cozy boot, like this platform ankle boot. Finally, throw on a long-sleeve top or sweater with a cute vest for an outfit that feels very fall.

Banana Republic The Icon Classic Wide-Leg Jean

Okay, you caught me—I actually wore this outfit for Christmas last year instead of Thanksgiving, but it definitely works for either holiday! For this combo, start with your favorite skirt and a turtleneck top. Then top it off with a relaxed-fitting blazer (I love this houndstooth blazer, but any pattern or solid color will do). On the bottom, throw on a pair of tights and a knee-high boot.

#5099. Singapore wants to test stablecoin payments by AI agents

The central bank plans to help develop a shared way to verify an agent’s authority. A separate sandbox would test safeguards for payments and corporate treasury.

Singapore’s central bank plans to help develop a common way for banks to verify who an AI agent represents and what the customer has authorized it to do. Chia Der Jiun, managing director of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), outlined the proposal on Nov. 19 at the Singapore FinTech Festival. A separate Singapore sandbox would test safeguards for AI agent payments, with stablecoins and tokenized deposits among the options.

Under the proposed know-your-agent protocol, a financial institution would receive information about the agent’s identity, the customer it acts for, its delegated authority and the rules it must follow. The protocol would also convey any assurances about the agent’s origin and reliability. The institution could use that information to set the scope of access and give the agent a dedicated, secure channel.

Chia said the customer’s mandate should specify the actions the agent may take and the limits and conditions on them. The more discretion the agent has or the greater the potential impact, the stronger the controls should be. MAS plans to help develop the protocol in the next phase of its Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime initiative.

MAS and the Future of Finance Institute announced the planned Agentic Money Sandbox on Nov. 18. The institute would set up a controlled environment for institutions to test payments and corporate treasury management with digital money ahead of any live deployment.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

Singapore has proposed a way to check an agent’s authority and separate sandbox trials for payments and corporate treasury.

The proposed payment trial would put the identity and authority checks at the bank or payment provider before execution.

The proposed treasury trial separates the company’s mandate from the bank’s terms for accepting an instruction.

The customer sets the mandate. The bank or payment provider sets controls before acting on an instruction.

MAS plans to help develop the protocol. The diagrams show the proposed trials and examples of digital money.

The arrows show who would pass an instruction to whom under the approach Chia Der Jiun outlined at the Singapore FinTech Festival on Nov. 19. The selectable views compare the two proposed trials.

MAS plans to help develop the protocol. The diagrams show the proposed trials and examples of digital money.

In the proposed payments test, the participating bank or payment provider would verify the agent’s identity and authority and apply risk controls before executing an instruction. Chia cited tokenized deposits and stablecoins as examples of the digital money the trial could use.

In the treasury test, a company would define what its agent could do. The agent could monitor cash balances and upcoming payments, decide when and where funds should move, and use tokenized deposits for permitted transfers. The bank would set its own controls and terms for accepting each instruction.

In a Nov. 18 speech, Singapore Deputy Prime Minister and MAS Chairman Gan Kim Yong gave the example of an agent making a payment under a contract once the relevant terms had been met and checked. The joint release named DBS, OCBC, Standard Chartered and UOB as the institute’s launch partners. The same release gave no sandbox start date or participant list.

Gan said institutions and companies remain accountable for actions taken on their behalf. Chia asked who bears responsibility when an agent makes a mistake or exceeds its mandate.

#5098. Anthropic Tops SpaceX's Initial IPO With $81 Billion Deal: Where the Money Went

Anthropic Tops SpaceX's Initial IPO With $81 Billion Deal: Where the Money Went

Anthropic has priced the largest initial IPO share sale in history at $81.34 billion, topping the $75 billion SpaceX first sold in June. But SpaceX still has the larger completed IPO after an additional share sale.

The Claude maker sold 980 million shares at $83 on Wednesday and is set to begin trading Thursday on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT.

The price beat the original $70-to-$78 range, while the company increased the offering from 825 million shares. Demand was about six times the number available before pricing.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perps on Decrypt.

At $83, Anthropic is valued at roughly $1.5 trillion including stock options and other potential shares, though its value based on outstanding shares is closer to $1.1 trillion.

The headline $81.34 billion isn't all money for Anthropic. About 956.35 million new shares bring $79.38 billion into the company before fees. Another 23.65 million shares, worth $1.96 billion, are being sold by its seven co-founders—roughly $280 million each. Anthropic receives none of that founders' cash, according to its final prospectus.

On top of the public sale, seven technology companies are buying $26 billion of nonvoting stock in a separate private placement. Google and Nvidia are putting in $10 billion each, AMD $2.5 billion, Broadcom, Micron and Microsoft $1 billion each, and TSMC $500 million.

The public offering and private placement total $107.34 billion in gross share sales, including the $1.96 billion going to founders rather than Anthropic.

The $104.8 billion net figure is for both transactions, not for the IPO alone. Anthropic gets $79.38 billion from its newly issued public shares, plus $26 billion from the private placement: $105.38 billion before costs. Subtract roughly $580 million in company-paid underwriting fees and estimated offering expenses, and the prospectus estimates $104.8 billion net.

That said, it could rise to about $117 billion if underwriters buy all the extra shares allowed. Anthropic plans to spend the money on operations, hiring and, above all, computing infrastructure.

Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley led a 22-bank underwriting group, with roughly $550 million in underwriting commissions. The company also offered access through brokers including Fidelity, Schwab, Robinhood, and SoFi, but retail investors received less than 20% of the offering.

Amazon remains the largest disclosed shareholder after the transaction with about 14.6% of the company, followed by Google at roughly 13.4%.

Early financial backers also hold enormous paper fortunes. Bloomberg estimates put Lightspeed's stake near $28 billion, Iconiq's above $26 billion and Menlo Ventures' around $22 billion. Ashton Kutcher's Sound Ventures reportedly holds shares worth almost $11 billion. Those figures are estimates of stock value, not cash they received at the IPO.

Investors, however, aren't buying much control. A special share class gives the founders' holding company 50.1% of shareholder voting power, while the Long-Term Benefit Trust can appoint a majority of the board.

So, Anthropic can raise historic sums while keeping key decisions largely away from ordinary shareholders.

Anthropic generated $33.24 billion in revenue during the first nine months of 2026, including $16.96 billion in the third quarter alone—the latest reported quarter. Its $81 billion annualized revenue run rate at the end of October projects recent customer spending over a year; it isn't money already earned.

Roughly 250 organizations now spend at least $10 million annually with Anthropic, and more than 1,900 spend at least $1 million, using trailing 12-month figures. Its net revenue retention reached about 900%.

In plain English, the same eligible customer group spent nine times as much in the latest three-month period as it did a year earlier. That measure excludes fixed-price Claude subscriptions.

But the business still depends on a few major accounts and distribution partners. Its five biggest customers generated about 25% of revenue over the first nine months of 2026, while cloud marketplaces accounted for 44%. In other words, companies like Amazon, Google and Microsoft can invest in Anthropic, provide the machines it runs on and help sell access to Claude.

Even the product changes at extraordinary speed: Claude models released during the six months through September made up more than 80% of third-quarter revenue. At the end of September 2026, Anthropic had about 5,300 employees and was generating more than $6.6 million in trailing annual revenue per employee.

Rapid growth doesn't mean easy profits. Anthropic posted a $567 million operating loss in the third quarter of 2026, after a $974 million operating profit in the second quarter. Over the first nine months, its operating loss totaled $1.26 billion. Those numbers tell a very different story from its much bigger headline net loss.

In the first nine months of 2026, Anthropic posted a $104.04 billion net loss, including $94.3 billion in noncash revaluations of convertible financing and related instruments. Yet it generated $6.57 billion in cash from operating activities during the same period. That is not free cash flow, which also accounts for capital spending, but the distinction matters: a $104 billion accounting loss does not mean $104 billion of cash burned.

The latest balance sheet, dated September 30, 2026, shows $95.6 billion in cash and equivalents plus $36.3 billion in short-term investments—$131.85 billion combined. Convertible notes payable stood at $130.50 billion at their accounting value, with some converting into shares around the IPO.

The final prospectus estimates $232.35 billion in cash and short-term investments on a pro forma, post-transaction basis. That last figure is a modeled balance after the offering and related adjustments, not cash the company held on September 30.

The more consequential number may be what it has promised to spend next. Anthropic disclosed about $900.9 billion in commitments, overwhelmingly for computing and infrastructure, stretching as far as 2045.

It separately estimates another $150 billion to $175 billion in payments under arrangements without fixed dollar amounts. Together, that points to potentially more than $1 trillion—but it is not a bill due today, and some contracts are conditional or can be terminated.

Some $70.7 billion of the stated commitments fall due in the 12 months after September 2026. That explains why even an IPO this large is not necessarily excessive capital for a frontier AI company. Every breakthrough attracts customers, but serving them requires more chips, power, and data centers.

There is a technical catch to the record. SpaceX's June IPO initially sold $75 billion in shares, but the final deal reached $86.25 billion gross after underwriters bought more shares—about $85.675 billion after fees, according to SpaceX's SEC filing.

Anthropic's $81.34 billion beats SpaceX's initial deal, not its final gross total. The extra $26 billion from Anthropic's private placement cannot be counted as public IPO proceeds. Its own option covers another 147 million shares worth about $12.2 billion; if exercised in full, its public IPO would reach $93.54 billion, comfortably above SpaceX's final figure.

Now attention turns to OpenAI. The ChatGPT maker recently raised $11 billion at a reported $1.25 trillion valuation and has indicated it will not list before 2027. Anthropic's debut offers a public-market test of what investors are willing to pay for AI revenue, while exposing the cost of generating it.

The interesting part isn't just that a five-year-old AI lab topped SpaceX's initial IPO. It's that it assembled more than $100 billion in combined public and private financing, started generating cash from operations—and still faces a potential trillion-dollar computing bill.

#5096. Aave’s $4 billion USDC borrow cap could leave just $190 million available for withdrawals

One wallet supplied more than a billion USDC to Aave’s Ethereum pool. The $190 million scenario assumes borrowing reaches the new cap and deposits stay at Friday’s level.

Aave raised its USDC borrow cap in the main Ethereum V3 market to $4 billion on Nov. 20, a day after one wallet deposited more than a billion USDC. Lenders had about 1.14 billion USDC available to withdraw late on Nov. 20. If borrowing hits the new cap and deposits stay at 4.19 billion USDC, about 190 million USDC would remain for withdrawals.

Aave's Ethereum Core market had 4.19 billion USDC supplied and 3.05 billion borrowed at 22:11 UTC on Nov. 20, according to an Aave API snapshot published by Aave Tracker. With 72.8% of the reserve lent out, subtracting the loans leaves about 1.14 billion USDC unborrowed. The same figures put borrowers about 950 million USDC below the new cap. That gap measures room under the borrowing limit.

The address, 0x176F…a132, supplied 400 million USDC and 350 million USDC in two transactions about eight minutes apart on Nov. 19. The same wallet received Aave's receipt tokens from both deposits.

Later that day, Aave raised the market's USDC deposit limit from 3.5 billion to 5 billion. LlamaRisk had reported that the old limit was 99.6% used. Four minutes and 24 seconds after the change, the same wallet supplied another 738 million USDC, bringing its deposits to 1,488 million USDC over about 75 minutes.

Coindaro reported that at 17:43 UTC on Nov. 19 the wallet held about 1.495 billion in aEthUSDC, the token that represents its deposits and accrued interest. At that same reading, the market had 4.228 billion USDC supplied and 2.604 billion borrowed, leaving roughly 1.62 billion unborrowed. At Ethereum block 26,459,205, just before 22:11 UTC on Nov. 20, on-chain balances showed the address holding about 1.495 billion aEthUSDC, or 35.7% of the receipt token's supply.

LlamaRisk recommended the higher borrowing limit on Nov. 20 after loans reached 98.5% of the previous $2.7 billion cap. Aave put the change into effect at 11:15 UTC. The amount of cash in the pool changes when users actually borrow, deposit, repay or withdraw.

At the late Nov. 20 supply of 4.19 billion USDC, the pool would have about 690 million left with 3.5 billion borrowed and 190 million left with 4 billion borrowed. The latter would put utilization at about 95.5%, above the 94% threshold where the variable borrowing rate starts to rise more steeply.

Anthropic Stock Opens 33% Above IPO Price as AI Stocks Rally

Anthropic shares opened at $111.50 on Thursday, approximately 33% above their $83 initial public offering price, as investors piled into the Claude developer on its highly anticipated Nasdaq debut.

Initial indications on the IPO open climbed from $108 earlier in the session, with successive price estimates reportedly moving closer together, Yahoo reported.

During the opening process, market makers and underwriters monitor incoming buy and sell orders to determine a price at which supply and demand can meet. Indications quickly climbed as Nasdaq established its official opening price.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

At $111, Anthropic commands a fully diluted valuation approaching $2 trillion, up from around $1.5 trillion at its IPO price. That represents nearly $500 billion in additional implied market value before its first public trade.

The excitement is spreading beyond Anthropic itself. U.S. stocks climbed Thursday, with semiconductor companies leading a broader rally in AI-related shares. Optical equipment makers, laser technology firms and neocloud providers also advanced, helping lift the technology sector as investors awaited Anthropic's first trade.

At the Nasdaq ceremony, Anthropic co-founders Dario and Daniela Amodei rang the opening bell, marking a milestone for one of the world's most prominent AI developers.

Daniela, who serves as the company's president, used the occasion to address people concerned about AI's growing influence.

"This technology needs you. Not your trust, not your use, but your voice," she said, urging the public to participate in shaping the technology's future.

"The end of the story isn't written yet. Intelligence is now something humans can build. What we choose to build with it is up to all of us," she added.

Anthropic priced 980 million shares at $83, raising $81.34 billion—more than SpaceX's initial $75 billion IPO, although still below its expanded final offering.

The debut follows a remarkable turnaround in sentiment. Just two weeks ago, some major investors were questioning whether Anthropic could sustain a $1.5 trillion valuation, with one suggesting it might need to accept something closer to $1 trillion.

For investors allocated shares at $83, a $110 opening translates into an immediate paper gain of $27 per share.

The bigger question is whether Anthropic's strong debut marks renewed confidence in the AI boom—or simply another example of investors paying increasingly extraordinary prices for its biggest names.

#5091. Russia allows Bitcoin trading as sanctioned Moscow Exchange prepares December launch

Russia is giving Bitcoin a place in brokerage accounts while its biggest exchange prepares to settle trades through a clearinghouse Washington sanctioned two years ago.

From Nov. 22, Russian exchanges can begin trading Bitcoin once the central bank approves the rules, but customers still can't use it to pay for anything.

Moscow Exchange plans a Dec. 1 pilot through a US-sanctioned clearinghouse, with ordinary investors limited to 300,000 rubles in annual purchases per intermediary.

The central bank's retail purchase rules took effect Nov. 17, limiting ordinary investors to Bitcoin, Ethereum and the dollar-linked stablecoin USDT. A separate ordinance governing exchange operations allows venues to begin trading from Nov. 22, provided the regulator has approved their trading rules.

Moscow Exchange aims to launch on Dec. 1, starting with pilot transactions as participating firms connect. The new market will let investors buy crypto through familiar financial intermediaries while prohibiting its use in everyday domestic payments.

The allowance covers purchases through a single intermediary during a calendar year.

If you buy 100,000 rubles' worth of Bitcoin and another 100,000 rubles' worth of Ethereum (about $1,200) through the same broker, you've used two-thirds of the allowance, regardless of what the coins are worth a week later.

Purchases can also go through asset managers and registered crypto exchange offices, including deals arranged outside an exchange's order book. The limit is measured in rubles spent on purchases, rather than the market value of the investor's holdings.

Qualified investors can buy other coins without the same purchase cap, although they must pass a test and review the risks before trading, just as ordinary investors do.

The central bank chose Bitcoin, Ethereum, and USDT for the retail list partly because they're heavily traded and have at least five years of price history on foreign exchanges.

Exchanges must register the companies trading there, track orders and completed transactions, calculate market prices, and report activity to the central bank.

Russia's new crypto law also provides for digital depositories that record asset ownership rights. They are part of the exchange and custody framework the new market will need once trading begins.

Owning Bitcoin through that system still won't let someone spend it at a Russian shop. Domestic merchants remain barred from accepting cryptocurrency for goods and services.

Exporters and importers can use it under a separate provision for cross-border settlement. A broker can help a customer exchange rubles for Bitcoin, and an exporter can receive Bitcoin for a shipment abroad, but a restaurant in Moscow still has to charge for lunch in something else.

Moscow Exchange already has a market for investors who want exposure to Bitcoin's price. By mid-September, it reported more than 600 billion rubles in crypto-futures turnover since its first contracts began trading in the summer of 2025.

Those cash-settled contracts pay gains or losses in rubles as crypto prices move, without delivering the underlying assets. The December pilot would trade the assets themselves, so the futures figure tells us little about how much Bitcoin investors will want to buy and hold through the new system.

The exchange's technical specification describes same-day and next-day settlement, while the National Clearing Centre's published market plan lists five trading pairs: Bitcoin, Ethereum, and USDT against rubles, plus Bitcoin and USDT against USDX, a specialized settlement currency used by the clearinghouse.

The exchange isn't planning direct BTC/USDT trading for the initial launch, although it may consider crypto-to-crypto pairs in 2027.

Members will be able to place anonymous orders or negotiate deals with known counterparties, and the clearinghouse expects to process settlements roughly every 30 to 60 minutes.

Short selling will initially be prohibited on the exchange, although brokers may offer margin trading under the applicable rules.

One large deal arranged in advance could lift the day's turnover without creating the steady stream of buyers and sellers that an ordinary investor needs.

The clearinghouse's FAQ also explains how the cryptocurrency will move once a trade is completed. Settlement will take place through accounts maintained at a separate digital depository outside the Moscow Exchange group, without a corresponding blockchain transaction for every trade.

When one participant buys Bitcoin from another, the depository can update its records of who holds the rights to those assets while the underlying coins stay in custody. That allows the exchange to process trades without sending Bitcoin between public wallets every time an order is matched.

The arrangement makes the depository's identity and the rules for moving assets into and out of its custody particularly important. Moscow Exchange has described the proposed account structure, but the published materials reviewed don't identify a separate depository or confirm whether customers can withdraw their holdings directly to personal wallets.

The market is initially intended for existing qualified trading and clearing participants, with brokers responsible for determining which customers can use their services.

Moscow Exchange says it will use the National Clearing Centre to clear the trades, relying on infrastructure already familiar to its stock-market participants.

The US Treasury sanctioned both Moscow Exchange and the National Clearing Centre in June 2024. That adds a complication for the planned USDT market, which the exchange intends to introduce initially through a pilot with restricted trading volumes.

The technical specification identifies USDT as issued on Ethereum, meaning a company outside Russia controls the underlying token. Tether has a policy for freezing wallets associated with people or entities on US sanctions lists, although that policy alone doesn't establish what will happen to any particular wallet used by Moscow Exchange or its clearing and custody partners.

Settling individual trades through depository accounts reduces the need to move tokens on a public blockchain, but the underlying USDT still has to be held somewhere.

The exchange hasn't identified the wallets that will hold those tokens, explained who will supply them, or described how Tether's sanctions controls would apply to the custody arrangement.

No freeze connected to the proposed pilot has been verified, and the available documents don't establish whether Tether has reviewed the arrangement.

The first trades in December may be deals clients already make elsewhere, brought onto Moscow Exchange's books.

If the pilot proceeds, repeat trading and the ability to buy or sell near the quoted price will tell us whether a usable market is taking shape.

For USDT, the exchange and its partners will also have to show they can hold the underlying tokens and complete settlement through the proposed depository, with the issuer's sanctions policy still unresolved.

#5090. Bitcoin Price Slips Near $61,500 as Tech Selloff Spreads to Asia

The bitcoin price slipped to near $61,500 on Friday morning, according to Look Into Bitcoin data, as a selloff in technology stocks that followed Anthropic’s Nasdaq debut spread to Asian markets and dragged bitcoin to its lowest level since July.

Bitcoin first broke below $62,000 on Thursday evening, after Thursday afternoon’s report showed it giving back a rebound toward $64,000. The bitcoin price then slid to nearly $61,200 during Asian trading before bouncing back above $61,700. Friday marks a third straight day of losses.

The selling started in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi slid more than 5%, with chipmakers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics down around 6%. The Korea Exchange halted program selling for five minutes after the drop, while Japan’s Nikkei fell as much as 4.85% to a seven-month low.

U.S. futures pointed lower too. Nasdaq-100 futures fell more than 1.7% and S&P 500 futures dropped 0.8%, Yahoo Finance reported. Gold futures lost 3%. The S&P 500 is pointing to a seventh straight daily decline, its longest losing streak since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.

Anthropic shares fell 8% in premarket trading after closing their first session at $97.17, up 17% from the $83 IPO price. Nvidia was down about 2.4% and AMD fell nearly 7%, CNBC reported. Hawkish signals from Federal Reserve officials this week also weighed on sentiment, Reuters said.

Bitcoin funds are feeling the pressure. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) recorded $541.1 million in net outflows on Thursday, its largest single-day outflow since launch. That topped the previous record of $528.3 million set on Jan. 30. The fund bled $2 billion over nine straight days of outflows earlier this month.

Leveraged traders took heavy losses as the bitcoin price broke support. Bitcoin liquidations hit $712.9 million over 24 hours, with $614 million coming from long positions. Open interest in bitcoin futures fell to $18 billion from $20 billion a week ago, and funding rates flipped broadly negative as traders unwound their bets.

Traders are now watching whether the bitcoin price can hold the $60,000 area. A large pocket of long positions sits in the $60,500 to $60,900 band, just below the current price, and could come into play on a further drop. Bitcoin is also on track for a seventh straight weekly loss, which would be its second-longest losing streak after nine weeks of declines in 2022.

Crypto stocks pointed lower in premarket trading. Strategy (MSTR) traded near $83.90, down about 2.6% from Thursday’s close of $86.13, after the stock fell for a sixth straight day on Thursday. Coinbase (COIN) slipped about 2.7% to near $106.

Bitcoin miners fell harder. IREN (IREN) dropped about 4.4%, CleanSpark (CLSK) lost about 3.6% and MARA Holdings (MARA) declined about 3.4%. Riot Platforms (RIOT) was down about 3.3%. IREN has also been under pressure as investors reassess AI infrastructure stocks. Delays in bringing some of its capacity online led Microsoft to spend less with the miner than planned last quarter.

Longer-term buyers have not left entirely. Institutional investors added 49,229 BTC through U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs in the third quarter, lifting their holdings to a record 356,491 BTC. Swiss bank Sygnum called the current downturn the shallowest bear market for bitcoin to date, putting the drawdown at around 54% compared with declines of more than 70% in previous cycles.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $61,800.

#5086. Hackers swapped a hosted DeepSeek model for 53 hours and stripped away its safety protections

Prime Intellect says the substitute ran on one deployment for 53 hours. It refused none of 240 harmful-request test prompts, compared with 198 for the original.

Prime Intellect disclosed an unauthorized DeepSeek model swap on Nov. 19. The host said a modified copy of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash served customer requests on one deployment for 53 hours. The substitute matched the original on two capability tests, the host said. On a safety test called HarmBench, refusals fell from 198 of 240 prompts to zero.

Prime Intellect said the affected deployment ran the substitute from 01:24 UTC on Nov. 8 until 06:35 UTC on Nov. 10, a window of 53 hours and 11 minutes. The company did not say how many requests went to that deployment during the swap.

The replacement used publicly available weights that Prime Intellect said had been modified to reduce refusals. Weights are the numerical settings that shape what a model generates. The swap took place behind the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash endpoint. Prime Intellect said the deployment kept its chat template and serving settings, along with the tokenizer that breaks text into pieces the model processes.

Prime Intellect reported unchanged results on GPQA Diamond and τ-bench when it tested the modified weights. GPQA Diamond tests advanced science questions, while τ-bench tests whether agents can use tools and follow rules in simulated customer interactions.

The safety tests exposed a difference. HarmBench was developed to evaluate how models respond to attempts to elicit harmful outputs. Prime Intellect also recorded a drop from 98 refusals out of 100 prompts to one on JailbreakBench, and from 304 out of 313 to two on StrongREJECT. The counts are from the company’s benchmark tests. The advisory gives no refusal count for customer requests.

Prime Intellect compared the original DeepSeek V4.1 Flash with the copy that served requests on one deployment for 53 hours.

A comparison limited to the two capability tests would have missed the fall in refusals.

The safety benchmarks use different prompt totals. Counts represent benchmark tests. The advisory does not provide individual capability scores or customer outcome counts.

Bars show reported refusals on a common count scale. Prime Intellect reported baseline totals of 240 HarmBench prompts, 100 JailbreakBench prompts and 313 StrongREJECT prompts. It described both capability results as unchanged.

The safety benchmarks use different prompt totals. Counts represent benchmark tests. The advisory does not provide individual capability scores or customer outcome counts.

Prime Intellect said it contacted all affected customers and advised those who relied on the model to refuse certain requests to review the outputs they received during the affected window. An answer from the substitute could have passed into an application that was counting on a refusal.

The company said it examined the disks and memory of the machines involved, checked recovered versions of the intruder’s proxy and reviewed records of their activity. It reported finding no evidence that customer prompts or responses were recorded or left the serving cluster. Prime Intellect also said no other models on its platform were modified and no keys or customer credentials were affected. Its investigation remains open.

#5085. Bitcoin Hovers Just Above Average Holder’s Cost Basis as Price Keeps Dipping

Bitcoin is trading just above its realized price, the average cost of every coin on the network, and a break below that level would put the average holder at a loss for the first time since early 2023, Glassnode, an onchain analytics firm posted Friday.

The price of bitcoin sat near $61,700 on Friday after sliding below $62,000. The realized price is a measure of what holders paid, not where the market trades. When bitcoin trades above it, the typical coin is sitting on a gain. Below it, the typical coin is underwater.

The margin is thin. The firm said the MVRV ratio, which compares bitcoin’s market value with its realized value, sits “just above 1.” A reading of 1 means the market price has fallen all the way to the realized price.

Realized price values each coin at the price it last moved on the blockchain, then averages across the supply. Look Into Bitcoin describes it as bitcoin’s average cost basis. Because it tracks the price when coins last changed hands, it moves far more slowly than the market.

The MVRV ratio expresses the same idea as a multiple. Above 1, holders are in profit on average. Below 1, they are not. A reading just above 1 means the market price is only a sliver higher than what the average coin cost.

The firm did not give the exact realized price in its post, which included a chart. That leaves the exact cushion between today’s price and the average cost basis unstated. Bitcoin Magazine Pro’s full realized price chart sits behind a login, so the current level could not be confirmed independently for this report.

“The average Bitcoin holder is still in profit,” the firm wrote. “The margin is thin.”

The slide has come with heavy selling from funds. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) lost about $541 million on Thursday, its largest one-day outflow since it launched in January 2024, Bloomberg reported. U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs lost about $582 million in total that day.

The selling stands out against the buying earlier in the fall. Institutions piled into bitcoin ETFs through the third quarter, pushing their combined holdings to a record, Bitcoin Magazine reported this week.

Leveraged traders took losses too. More than $700 million in leveraged crypto positions were liquidated over 24 hours, and about 86% of them were bets on higher prices. Bitcoin accounted for roughly $200 million of the total.

CoinShares head of research James Butterfill said the drop is part of a longer downturn rather than the start of a new one. “I see this as a continuation of the existing bear market rather than the start of another,” he said in a note dated Nov. 18.

The note frames Friday’s price action as a late stage of a decline that began well before November. Butterfill pointed to whale selling that weighed on prices from late 2025, expectations of higher interest rates and weakness in technology stocks, all of which have kept buyers cautious.

“Our base case remains range trading around USD 60k to 90k through much of 2027, until falling inflation gives monetary policy room to ease,” he said. “Geopolitics will have a considerable say in that.”

A move through the realized price would put bitcoin near the bottom edge of that range. The firm said holders as a group have not been in loss since early 2023.

A sustained breakout, Butterfill said, would likely require “a change in the policy outlook, renewed whale participation or both.”

#5083. What Are Perpetual Futures? How Crypto's Most Popular Derivative Works

What Are Perpetual Futures? How Crypto's Most Popular Derivative Works

Perpetual futures are the engine room of crypto trading. Centralized exchanges processed $85.3 trillion in perps trading volume in 2025 alone, according to CoinGecko's State of Crypto Perpetuals Report 2026, and the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) describes perps as the dominant form of crypto derivatives trading.

They aren't only for crypto, either. Exchanges now offer perps on stocks, commodities and currencies, and Decrypt has become the first news publisher to offer perps trading, powered by Solana exchange Phoenix.

This guide explains what futures are, what makes perpetual futures different, how funding rates and liquidations work, and what to know before trading them.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

To understand perpetual futures, it helps to start with ordinary futures.

A futures contract is an agreement to buy or sell an asset at a set price on a set date in the future. Futures have been used for centuries: farmers used them to lock in prices for crops before harvest, and today they are traded on everything from oil and wheat to stock indexes and Bitcoin, on regulated exchanges such as CME.

Traders use futures for two main reasons. Hedgers use them to protect against price swings; an airline might buy oil futures to lock in fuel costs, for example. Speculators use them to bet on price movements without owning the underlying asset.

Traditional futures have an expiry date. When a contract expires, it settles, either by delivering the asset or, more often, by paying out the difference in cash. Traders who want to keep their position open must "roll" it into a new contract, which can add costs and complexity.

Perpetual futures, often shortened to "perps" or "perpetual swaps," work like futures, but with one key difference: they never expire. Traders can hold a position for as long as they like, provided they have enough collateral to keep it open.

The idea was proposed by Yale economist Robert Shiller in a 1993 paper as a way to create markets for assets that are hard to trade directly. Perps took off in crypto. Crypto exchange BitMEX, widely credited with bringing perps to crypto, launched a perpetual contract on Bitcoin in 2016. BitMEX itself closed in September 2026, but the product it pioneered has become the most traded instrument in crypto.

A perpetual contract never actually involves owning the asset. Traders deposit collateral, or "margin," and their profit or loss depends entirely on how the price moves.

When opening a perp position, a trader chooses a direction. Going long means betting the price will rise; going short means betting it will fall. Being able to short as easily as going long is one reason perps are popular: it lets traders profit from falling prices, or hedge assets they already own.

Perps are usually traded with leverage, which lets traders control a larger position than their collateral alone would allow. With 10x leverage, for example, $100 of margin controls a $1,000 position. If the asset's price rises 5%, the trader makes $50, a 50% return on their margin. But if it falls 5%, they lose $50, half of their margin.

Exchanges track two prices to manage this. The index price is the asset's price on spot markets, usually averaged across several exchanges. The mark price, based on the index and the perp market itself, is used to calculate profits and losses and to decide when positions must be closed. Using an averaged price makes it harder for a sudden spike on one exchange to trigger liquidations.

Because perps never expire, nothing forces their price to converge with the underlying asset, as traditional futures do at expiry. Instead, perps use a funding rate.

At regular intervals—most commonly every eight hours, though some platforms use shorter or longer schedules—traders on one side of the market pay traders on the other:

Decentralized exchange Hyperliquid, for example, pays funding every hour, at one-eighth of the rate calculated for an eight-hour period, to stay consistent with centralized exchanges.

Funding payments go directly between traders, not to the exchange. For traders holding positions over long periods, these payments can add up, and they can either boost or erode returns.

Funding rates also offer a window into market sentiment. Strongly positive funding suggests traders are crowded into bullish bets, while negative funding shows that bears are paying to stay short.

Rates for the same asset can also differ between exchanges. On November 19, 2026, Bitcoin's funding rate was 0.01% per eight hours on Hyperliquid, compared with 0.0037% on Binance, according to Hyperliquid's funding comparison tool.

Some traders aim to earn funding payments rather than bet on prices. In a "cash and carry" or basis trade, they buy an asset on the spot market and short the same amount through perps, collecting funding while their positions offset each other's price moves.

Leverage is a double-edged sword. Every perp position has a maintenance margin, the minimum collateral needed to keep it open. If losses push a trader's margin below that level, the exchange automatically closes the position, a process called liquidation. The trader typically loses most or all of the margin they put up.

The higher the leverage, the smaller the price move needed to trigger a liquidation. At 50x leverage, a 2% move against a position can wipe it out.

Liquidations can also feed on each other. When prices fall sharply, liquidated longs are forced to sell, pushing prices lower and triggering further liquidations, a so-called liquidation cascade. On October 10, 2025, the crypto market saw its largest liquidation event on record, with more than $19 billion in leveraged positions wiped out in a single day.

To cover losses when positions can't be closed in time, exchanges typically keep an insurance fund. In extreme cases, some use auto-deleveraging, closing profitable positions on the other side of the market to keep the system solvent.

Crypto perps trade on two main types of venue.

Centralized exchanges, such as Binance, Bybit and OKX, run their own order books and hold users' funds. They account for the vast majority of perps trading: Binance alone held about a third of centralized perps volume in early 2026, according to CoinGecko. Many are unavailable to U.S. customers.

Decentralized exchanges let traders use perps through smart contracts, while keeping control of their funds. Some, such as Hyperliquid and Solana-based Phoenix, run order books onchain, matching buyers and sellers much like a traditional exchange. Others, such as GMX and Jupiter, let traders trade against a shared pool of liquidity provided by other users.

Decentralized perps are growing fast. Their trading volume jumped from $1.5 trillion in 2024 to $6.38 trillion in 2025, led by Hyperliquid, CoinGecko found. Decentralized exchanges' share of perps trading volume peaked at 13% in late 2025 before slipping to 10% in April 2026, while their share of open interest, the total value of open positions, reached 13.5%.

In the U.S., perps developed largely on offshore exchanges, outside the reach of the CFTC, but that has started to change. In July 2025, Coinbase introduced CFTC-regulated "perpetual-style" futures for U.S. customers, with five-year expiries and up to 10x leverage. Two months later, CFTC-regulated exchange Bitnomial launched what it called the first U.S. perpetual futures, with 25-year terms and eight-hour funding. In May 2026, the CFTC approved a Bitcoin perpetual futures contract from prediction market Kalshi and set out a framework for listing more, and in June, Kraken rolled out perps to eligible U.S. customers through Bitnomial, which its parent company had acquired.

Some of these contracts, including Kalshi's and Bitnomial's original design, have long but fixed terms of 25 years, so are not strictly perpetual. The regulator says perps can be offered on CFTC-registered exchanges under federal oversight, and has advised U.S. traders to avoid offshore venues.

The shift has been contested. CME Group, the largest U.S. futures exchange, has sued the CFTC, arguing that perps are swaps rather than futures under U.S. law. The CFTC has nonetheless continued to approve more perps platforms, starting with Backpack.

Perps are now spreading beyond crypto. Exchanges have begun listing perps tracking stocks, stock indexes, commodities such as gold and oil, and currencies, giving traders around-the-clock exposure to markets that normally close in the evening and on weekends.

Those products carry the same mechanics, and the same risks, as crypto perps. They track an asset's price without giving traders ownership of the asset itself, so a perp on a company's stock doesn't come with voting rights or dividends.

Perps can be useful tools for hedging and speculation, but they are among the riskiest products in crypto:

Decrypt users can now trade perps directly alongside the news, through the Decrypt Money Account. The service is powered by Phoenix, a decentralized exchange on Solana, and lets users go long or short on crypto, stocks and commodities.

Availability varies by region, and as with any leveraged product, traders should only risk money they can afford to lose.

#5081. Block Says Most Bitcoin Payments on Square Are for Coffee and Food

Most bitcoin payments at Square sellers are small, everyday purchases at coffee shops and restaurants, Block said in a new report that it hopes will inform a debate in Congress over a tax break for small crypto purchases.

The report, “The State of Bitcoin Payments,” covers completed bitcoin payments at U.S. Square sellers from Nov. 1, 2025, to Oct. 15, 2026. The median payment was about $13, and the average was about $29.

Food and drink businesses took 72% of those payments, Block found. That is a bigger share than the category’s 67.5% slice of regular card payments on Square over the same period.

“Most bitcoin payments are small and routine,” the company wrote on X Thursday, calling the report one of the first datasets on how people spend bitcoin in the local economy.

Coffee shops and fast food businesses accounted for 62.6% of the bitcoin payments in the food and drink category, with a median payment of $9.10. Grocery stores made up a smaller share but had the highest average payment in the group, at $60.73.

Small tickets dominated. About 42% of bitcoin payments on Square were under $10, and 65.1% were under $20. Those sub-$20 payments made up just 19.1% of total payment value, though, with a few larger purchases accounting for much of the dollars spent.

Customers also came back. Among Cash App users who paid with bitcoin at least twice at the same merchant, the median was three purchases per customer-merchant pair. About 44% of bitcoin payments from Cash App were repeat payments, and 86% of those came within 30 days.

The activity was not limited to Block’s own app. External Lightning wallets such as Strike, Wallet of Satoshi, Phoenix and Coinbase handled 56.6% of Square bitcoin payments and about 66% of payment value, while Cash App wallets made up the rest.

Square sellers can choose how much of each sale they keep in bitcoin, and Square converts the rest to dollars automatically. Block said zero-fee processing for bitcoin payments on Square has been extended through Dec. 31, 2027. Local governments are testing similar setups, with Miami-Dade County now taking bitcoin for property taxes and converting it to dollars.

Block tied the data to tax policy. Under current U.S. federal rules, paying with bitcoin generally means calculating a capital gain or loss on every purchase, even a $10 coffee, the company said.

A Morning Consult survey that Block commissioned found that 23.6% of businesses that don’t accept bitcoin cite tax and accounting complexity as a reason. That is about the same share that cite regulation, refunds or price swings. Among businesses that have considered taking bitcoin but haven’t, the figure was 27%.

Consumers pointed to friction, too. Morning Consult surveyed 8,669 U.S. adults who are aware of bitcoin in August. Among those who don’t own it, 29.6% said they would be more likely to pay with bitcoin if it were easier, and 15.7% of that group said they were unsure how it is taxed or regulated.

Block said Congress is weighing a crypto tax package and pointed to a de minimis exemption, which would exempt small gains on qualifying purchases, as one option. Industry groups have pressed lawmakers on crypto tax rules for months, with little movement so far.

The report doesn’t give totals. Block said the number of Square bitcoin payments, the number of sellers receiving them and total bitcoin payment volume are proprietary and not disclosed. Merchant lists like the 425 Los Angeles businesses that accept bitcoin offer a rough sense of reach.

“We think tax policy should account for how people spend bitcoin as well as how they hold it,” Block said.

#5080. Ripple’s Alderoty doubts Elizabeth Warren will ‘set crypto policy in this country,’ backs durable agency rules

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Alderoty downplayed Warren’s influence, backing durable agency rules, and urging crypto groups to unify their message to Congress.

Ripple Chief Legal Officer Stuart Alderoty is looking to federal regulators to carry crypto market rules over the finish line, arguing that Elizabeth Warren's expected rise to lead the Senate Banking Committee won't put her in charge of the industry's future.

"I don’t think Elizabeth Warren is going to set crypto policy in this country," Alderoty said at The Hill and The Block’s Capitol Crypto Forum on Thursday. "She'll probably focus on oversight and hearings, which I think will be a short-term distraction."

Alderoty, who also serves as president of the National Cryptocurrency Association, said he expects other lawmakers to take the wheel on crypto policy over Warren, who he described as "overtly anti-crypto."

Despite this, he does not expect a version of the Clarity Act to be reintroduced in the coming Congress, pointing to a packed legislative calendar and the 2028 presidential election as priorities.

Pieces of the proposal could be folded into tax legislation or other bills, he said, but a broader bill would likely struggle to garner the committee support needed to reach the floor.

"I think the emphasis and the focus is going to move to the SEC and the CFTC," Alderoty said, also mentioning collaborations with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.

Asked whether action from those agencies would be enough for the industry over the next two years without market structure legislation, Alderoty said: "I think it's enough, and I think it's really important."

He argues that rules created through public comment and data analysis would be difficult for a future administration to reverse because they would need to carry out their own policymaking and justify disrupting the market's reliance on the existing rules, he said.

Alderoty contrasted that with the approach taken by former SEC Chair Gary Gensler, arguing that reliance on enforcement left little to no durable policy when he left.

"The Gensler SEC did not do the hard work of rulemaking," he said. "What they decided to do was fall back to regulation by enforcement."

"This administration is doing the hard work of rulemaking, and that is durable," he added.

Alderoty also pushed crypto companies to improve how they present their priorities to Congress.

He cited a handful of possible reasons for the breakdown in the Clarity Act's passage, including the Senate's decision not to advance the House-passed bill, the schism between stablecoin and market structure legislation and disputes over rewards. Ethics concerns surrounding the Trump family’s crypto ties ultimately "overwhelmed the conversation," he said.

The industry's competing messages also made things murky, he added, with different groups and companies all going after lawmakers with "esoteric issues" on DeFi, stablecoin rewards, and token classifications.

When you consider that lawmakers' understanding of crypto can vary widely, it makes the industry's more technical pitches hard to follow. Alderoty likened the situation to a policymaker telling him about fishermen coming in to discuss fishing laws, tackle and tides that the lawmaker didn't understand.

"We need to do the hard work of seeing what do we agree on, making that clear," Alderoty said.

Despite the setbacks, he urged the industry to continue working across party lines.

"Crypto is a policy issue," Alderoty said. "It's not a political issue."

#5075. Kalshi’s Quintenz says insider trading is ‘just easier to see’ in prediction markets than stocks

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Kalshi board member Brian Quintenz said there are far more insider trading cases in the stock market, but the link between a trader and an event's outcome can be easier to see in prediction markets.

Brian Quintenz, Kalshi board member and former commissioner of the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, said there are far more insider trading cases in the stock market than in prediction markets, where it can be easier to see when someone has affected the outcome of an event they traded on.

"And there are by far more insider trading cases that happen in the stock market than anything that happens in the derivatives markets or in the prediction market space," Quintenz said Thursday at The Hill and The Block's Capitol Crypto Forum. "It's just easier to see because it's very direct."

Quintenz said the possibility of insider trading should not make a market illegal or invalid. He said enforcement after a violation should supplement the work exchanges do to prevent it, and added that there was more work to do.

Dan Berkovitz, vice chair of external and regulatory affairs at Millennium Management and a former CFTC commissioner, said federal and exchange rules already prohibit insider trading. He said exchanges also need rules on who can trade, including employees of organizations involved in a contract and people who can influence its outcome.

"So you need rules against insider trading, you need participation limits, and you need strict anti-manipulation provisions," Berkovitz said.

Berkovitz pointed to mention markets, where the outcome can depend on whether a person says a particular word or phrase. A person who can decide whether to say something can also decide the outcome of the contract, he said. Berkovitz welcomed the CFTC's guidance but said more work is needed on who has insider information or can influence the outcome.

"Who has influence or control of the contract? Who has insider knowledge? Those types of things, I think we can still use further development, but there's initial steps being taken to get there," Berkovitz said.

Christy Goldsmith Romero, senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and a former CFTC commissioner, said exchanges are the first line of defense against insider trading and that the CFTC probably needs to do more. She pointed to the requirement that exchanges certifying their own contracts attest that those contracts are not readily susceptible to manipulation. She added that greater clarity was needed from the CFTC to assist exchanges with that.

Quintenz agreed that more guidance would help. However, he said whether a contract is readily susceptible to manipulation is a judgment call and that the CFTC should explain how it applies the standard rather than leaving exchanges to come up with different standards on their own.

The panel also discussed who should regulate sports event contracts. Berkovitz explained that the post-Dodd-Frank final rule continues to prohibit gaming contracts via the CFTC, subject only to future regulatory amendment. The latest interim rule, however, draws a distinction between gambling conducted at a casino and products listed for trading on a federally regulated exchange, Berkovitz said. He added that a legal question remains over whether essentially the same product can be treated as a swap on one platform but not another.

Quintenz said he had submitted a comment letter in his personal capacity, noting that the Supreme Court's 2018 sports betting ruling did not give states exclusive authority. He said federal regulators can oversee exchanges and states can continue regulating casinos and sportsbooks.

Meanwhile, Goldsmith Romero said the Supreme Court would likely take up the matter given the conflicting decisions across the Circuit Courts. "I think it's likely that the prediction markets may end up losing on the sports contracts," she said.

She also said the Securities and Exchange Commission could become more involved as prediction markets offer more contracts related to public companies and their stocks. She added that it would also help if both the SEC and CFTC worked together to provide more clarity.
